Design Brief · Working Reference

Diarsa Global — Website Research & Direction

Compiled from a full teardown of Diarsa's current site plus three reference firms — Mott MacDonald, AEC Group, and Julius Berger Nigeria. Everything below is what we're carrying forward, what we're deliberately leaving behind, and what we still need from the MD before building starts.

The Direction
Mott MacDonald's restraint and system discipline, executed with Julius Berger's local warmth and confidence — built for a Nigerian audience that won't wade through corporate abstraction. The design does the convincing; the words stay simple, direct, and concrete. Diarsa doesn't have a global reputation to lean on yet, so the site has to earn trust through real proof — real projects, real people, real numbers — not brand poetry.
Reference Sites — Scorecard
Mott MacDonald
Reference standard

Not directly comparable — a 40,000+ person global consultancy. Used as a pattern library for structure, restraint, and system discipline, not a template to scale-copy.

AEC Group
6/10

Strong tagline and real named local projects, undermined by maze-like navigation, a hero that explains almost nothing, a generic WordPress build, and a scroll/preload bug from a heavy slider plugin.

Julius Berger
7/10

Best hero concept of the three (a real, iconic local landmark) and the strongest credibility content — a real founding year, named milestones, named certifications. Let down by a broken, empty-feeling mobile hero.

Principles To Carry Forward

Organized by what each one actually governs — not a flat list, since some of these are structural rules and some are just good habits worth repeating.

Navigation & Structure

  • Every top-level label must be self-explanatory alone — no vague identity words like "Our Firm" that require a click to understand.
  • One dropdown level, maximum. Direct one-click links wherever the destination is obvious.
  • 5–7 primary nav items. Berger's 8 is already pushing it; AEC's nested maze is the failure case to avoid entirely.
  • Nav controls (menu, search, contact) sit on the right — matches convention, reads calmer.
  • Selecting a menu item should transition cleanly into that section, not leave a pile of competing options on screen (Berger's push-menu vs. AEC's sprawl).
  • Every link must actually go somewhere. Diarsa's current "#!" placeholders are the single biggest credibility killer on the existing site — fix this before anything else.

Imagery & Identity

  • Hero image should be one real, locally-recognizable landmark — ideally in Edo/Benin City, tied to where Diarsa already has real government relationships, not generic stock.
  • Use actual Diarsa people and real project photography. Authentic representation reads as trust in a way stock imagery never will.
  • Drone footage is a real asset Diarsa has that most local competitors don't — plan a shoot around whichever flagship projects get chosen for the Projects page.
  • A Nigerian flag as a quiet identity/pride marker, placed at the close of the site (footer) — not scattered throughout.
  • Two overlapping photos (a small one peeking from behind a larger one) is a cheap, repeatable way to add visual depth without custom art per section.

Color & Type

  • Three-color 60/30/10 system — one dominant neutral, one secondary, one confident accent. Discipline, not variety, is what reads as expensive.
  • Structure needs contrast to read as structure — a divider line on a busy or pale background disappears; on a considered ground it reads as intentional.
  • Oversized section headers paired with exactly one clear supporting line — scannable, not paragraph-heavy.

Layout & Motion

  • Consistent, predictable section rhythm (block, image, block, image) so a visitor can almost guess what comes next — reads as composed, not assembled.
  • True symmetry and alignment at every breakpoint — phone, tablet, laptop, wide desktop. Not just "doesn't break" — actually composed at each size.
  • CTA buttons invert contrast cleanly against whatever background they land on.
  • A closing "bookend" brand statement that appears consistently in every page's footer.
  • Simple, purposeful scroll-reveal motion only. No heavy legacy slider plugins — the AEC lesson: fast load, no preloader gating content, no scroll jank.
  • Service/expertise cards need an actual invitation to click — a hover response, active microcopy ("Explore Buildings →") — description alone isn't enough to earn the click.

Content & Copy

  • Simple, direct wording over corporate abstraction. Diarsa doesn't have Mott MacDonald's reputation yet, so the words have to do more of the convincing.
  • Real, named, recognizable local projects front and center — the single strongest trust signal available, stronger than any design choice.
  • A real timeline with specific named milestones (if Diarsa has one) beats vague "years of excellence" every time — specificity is what makes a claim feel true.
  • Name certifications and registrations specifically (COREN, ISO, whatever's real) rather than vague "certified."
  • A tight, memorable framing for the four service areas — a clean, verb-led breakdown, the way AEC frames Plan / Design / Supervise.
  • Publish fewer, substantial pieces in News/Insights rather than frequent thin filler — this was Diarsa's original weakness (three near-identical posts).
  • Action-phrased CTA copy ("Start your project today") over sterile button text ("Submit Inquiry").

Deliberately Skip

  • No literal financial/annual-report disclosure page — a lighter "Company Profile" download or a simple stats strip does the same trust-building job.
  • No multi-office locator system — one address and a map inside Contact is enough at this scale.
  • No Investor Relations / AGM / shareholder machinery — that exists because Berger is publicly listed on the NSE. Diarsa isn't.
  • No multi-country language toggle unless there's real cross-border work to justify it — confirm with the MD first.
  • No video production to match Mott MacDonald — shelve for post-launch, keep it simple whenever it happens.
  • No filler "we care"-style sections that pad the site's length without adding a real decision-driver.
Recommended Page Structure
Home→ About→ Services→ Projects→ Industries Served→ Testimonials→ FAQ→ Careers→ Contact / Quote
About holds team, vision/mission, real history, and values. Careers leads with achievements, then a dedicated "build your career" moment — not the MD's face first. Contact routes by inquiry type (Quote / Careers / General) so nothing lands in the wrong inbox.
What We Need From the MD

The consolidated ask — everything below turns this brief into an actual build.

Brand

  • Logo file and brand colors — or the green light to define these fresh, the way we did for Divine Forge.
  • Any existing brand guide beyond the logo.

Company Facts

  • Founding year and real history/milestones — decade-by-decade if possible.
  • Real numbers: years operating, projects completed, team size, states/regions covered.
  • Certifications and registrations, named specifically (COREN, etc.).
  • Awards or recognitions, if any.
  • Company values — ideally something memorable, the way Mott MacDonald's "PRIDE" works as an acronym.
  • Whether any real cross-border or regional work exists (decides the language-toggle question).
  • Whether Diarsa has partner firms or subsidiaries worth surfacing.

People

  • MD's name, short bio, and headshot.
  • Team bios and photos for whoever should be featured per specialty (Civil, Geomatics, Environmental, R&D).

Projects

  • Which flagship projects to prioritize for the Projects page.
  • Per project: name, location, client, scope of work, timeline, the challenge and how Diarsa solved it, real photos, Diarsa's specific role, and key numbers.
  • Confirm the hero landmark choice — ideally in Edo/Benin City, tied to a real Diarsa relationship.
  • Plan a drone shoot around whichever projects get chosen.

Content & Messaging

  • Real client testimonials.
  • Real FAQ questions and answers.
  • What message the MD wants to send in a "stay informed" / newsletter-style section.
